title: No. 7 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers from Dissensions Between the States) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: People sometimes ask, with an air of triumph, what reasons the States would have to make war on each other if they were disunited. A complete answer would be: precisely the same reasons that have, at various times, drowned all the nations of the world in blood. But unfortunately for us, the question allows a more specific answer. There are causes of conflict already in plain view, and we have enough experience—even under the restraints of a federal constitution—to judge what we could expect if those restraints were removed.

Territorial disputes have always been one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. Probably the largest share of wars that have devastated the earth have sprung from this cause. The same cause would exist among us in full force. We have a vast tract of unsettled territory within the boundaries of the United States. Several States already have rival, unresolved claims, and dissolving the Union would lay the foundation for similar claims among all of them. They have already had serious and heated arguments about the rights to lands that were ungranted at the time of the Revolution—usually called the crown lands. The States within whose colonial governments those lands fell have claimed them as their property. The other States have argued that the rights of the crown in this matter passed to the Union—especially as to all the western territory which, by actual possession or by submission of the Indian proprietors, fell under the jurisdiction of the king of Great Britain until it was surrendered in the peace treaty. That, it has been said, was in any case an acquisition by the Confederacy through compact with a foreign power. Congress has prudently tried to defuse this controversy by persuading the States to cede such lands to the United States for the benefit of all. Under a continuing Union, this approach has gone far enough to make a peaceful end of the dispute likely. But breaking up the Confederacy would revive this dispute and create others on the same subject. At present, much of the vacant western territory is, by cession at least—if not by any prior right—the common property of the Union. If the Union ended, the States that made the cessions on a federal compromise would likely reclaim those lands as a reversion, since the reason for the grant would have ceased. The other States would surely insist on a share, by right of representation. Their argument would be that a grant once made cannot be revoked, and that the justice of sharing in territory acquired or secured by the joint efforts of the Confederacy remained intact. Even if every State improbably agreed that each had a right to a share of this common stock, the question of a fair rule of apportionment would still be a hurdle. Different States would propose different principles, and since these would clash with the opposing interests of the parties, peaceful adjustment might not come easily.

In the broad field of western territory, then, we see plenty of room for hostile claims, with no umpire or common judge to step between the contending parties. Reasoning from the past to the future, we have good reason to fear that the sword would sometimes be appealed to as the arbiter of their differences. The dispute between Connecticut and Pennsylvania over the land at Wyoming warns us not to be optimistic about easy settlements of such disagreements. The Articles of Confederation required the parties to submit the matter to a federal court. The submission was made, and the court ruled in favor of Pennsylvania. But Connecticut showed strong signs of dissatisfaction with that ruling, and she did not seem fully reconciled to it until something like compensation for her supposed loss was found through negotiation. Nothing here is meant to cast even the slightest blame on that State. She no doubt sincerely believed she had been wronged by the decision, and States, like individuals, accept rulings against their own interests only with great reluctance.

Those who saw the inside of the controversy between this State and the district of Vermont can confirm the opposition we faced—from States with no stake in the claim as well as those that had one—and can testify to the danger our Confederacy's peace might have run if this State had tried to assert its rights by force. Two motives drove that opposition. One was a wariness of our future power. The other was the interest of certain influential individuals in the neighboring States, who had obtained land grants under the actual government of that district. Even the States that brought forward their own claims against ours seemed more eager to dismember this State than to make good their own pretensions. These were New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. New Jersey and Rhode Island, on every occasion, showed warm zeal for Vermont's independence. Maryland did the same, until alarmed by signs of a connection between Canada and that State. As small States, they viewed the prospect of our growing greatness with an unfriendly eye. Reviewing these episodes, we can trace some of the causes that would likely embroil the States with each other if they had the misfortune to become disunited.

Commercial competition would be another fertile source of conflict. The States with less favorable circumstances would seek to escape the disadvantages of their location and share in the advantages of their luckier neighbors. Each State, or separate confederacy, would pursue its own commercial policy. This would create distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, and these would breed discontent. The habits of trade on equal terms, which we have known since the country was first settled, would sharpen these grievances even more than they would have on their own. WE WOULD BE QUICK TO LABEL AS INJURIES WHAT WERE REALLY THE LEGITIMATE ACTS OF INDEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTIES PURSUING THEIR OWN INTERESTS. The spirit of enterprise that marks America's commercial class has never let an opportunity go unused. It is unlikely that this unbridled spirit would respect the trade regulations by which particular States might try to secure exclusive benefits for their own citizens. Violations of these regulations on one side, and the efforts to prevent and punish them on the other, would naturally lead to outrages, then to reprisals, then to wars.

The chances some States would have to make others tributary through commercial regulations would be borne with impatience by the tributary States. The relative situation of New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey would be a clear example. New York, needing revenue, must impose duties on her imports. A large share of those duties must be paid by the inhabitants of the two other States as consumers of what we import. New York would not be willing or able to give up this advantage. Her citizens would not agree to refund a duty they had paid in favor of the citizens of her neighbors. Even if they wanted to, it would be impractical to distinguish those customers in our own markets. Would Connecticut and New Jersey long submit to being taxed by New York for her exclusive benefit? Should we be allowed to keep undisturbed possession of a metropolis whose advantage was so odious to our neighbors and, in their view, so oppressive? Could we hold it against the weight of Connecticut on one side and the cooperating pressure of New Jersey on the other? Only recklessness would answer these questions yes.

The Union's public debt would be another cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. Both the initial apportionment and the gradual paying-off afterward would breed ill humor and resentment. How could the States ever agree on a rule of apportionment that satisfied everyone? Hardly any rule that could be proposed is entirely free of real objections. As usual, those objections would be magnified by the opposing interests of the parties. The States even disagree on the general principle of paying off the public debt. Some, either less impressed by the importance of national credit or because their citizens have little immediate stake in the question, feel indifference—if not outright reluctance—to paying the domestic debt at any rate. These States would be inclined to magnify the difficulties of distribution. Others, with many citizens who hold a disproportionate share of the national debt as creditors, would push hard for some fair and effective provision. The procrastinations of the first group would stir resentment in the second. Meanwhile, the settlement of a rule would be delayed by real disagreement and deliberate stalling. The citizens of the interested States would clamor. Foreign powers would press for satisfaction of their just demands. And the peace of the States would be put at risk by the double threat of foreign invasion and internal conflict.

Suppose the difficulty of agreeing on a rule were overcome and the apportionment made. There would still be plenty of reason to expect that the rule, in practice, would bear harder on some States than on others. Those who suffered would naturally seek to ease the burden. The others would just as naturally resist a revision likely to increase their own load. Their refusal would be too convenient an excuse for the complaining States to withhold their contributions—they would seize on it eagerly. And those States' non-compliance with their obligations would be a ground for bitter argument and quarrel. Even if the rule adopted in practice lived up to its principle of equality, delinquencies in payment from some States would still result from various other causes: real lack of resources, mismanagement of finances, accidental disorders in government, and—on top of all that—the reluctance people generally feel to part with money for purposes that have outlived the urgent needs that produced them and that interfere with the supply of immediate wants. Delinquencies, from whatever causes, would breed complaints, accusations, and quarrels. Perhaps nothing is more likely to disturb the tranquility of nations than being bound to mutual contributions for some common purpose that does not yield an equal and matching benefit. For it is an observation as true as it is well-worn, that there is nothing people are quicker to fight about than the payment of money.

Laws that violate private contracts, since they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them, may be considered another probable source of hostility. We have no reason to expect that a more liberal or fairer spirit will preside over the laws of the individual States in the future—if unrestrained by additional checks—than we have already seen in too many cases disgracing their codes. We have noticed the disposition to retaliation aroused in Connecticut as a result of the outrages committed by the Legislature of Rhode Island. We can reasonably infer that in similar cases, under other circumstances, a war—not of PARCHMENT, but of the sword—would punish such atrocious breaches of moral obligation and social justice.

The probability of incompatible alliances between the different States or confederacies and different foreign nations, and the effects of that on the peace of the whole, have been laid out fully enough in earlier papers. From the view they have given of this part of the subject, the conclusion is this: America, if not connected at all, or connected only by the weak tie of a simple offensive and defensive league, would—through the operation of such clashing alliances—be gradually drawn into all the destructive mazes of European politics and wars. And through the destructive disputes among the parts into which she had been divided, she would likely fall prey to the schemes and machinations of powers that were equally enemies of them all. Divide et impera(1) must be the motto of every nation that either hates or fears us.(2)

2. So that the entire subject of these papers may be laid before the public as soon as possible, it is proposed to publish them four times a week—on Tuesday in the New York Packet and on Thursday in the Daily Advertiser.
